overview: Wet systems keep rolling in off the Pacific all week. The Coast Mountains get the most snow early in the week, and the Cascades see several rounds of mixed rain and snow with the strongest push Wednesday. The Northern Rockies stay quieter until a stronger westerly flow arrives Thursday into Friday.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Snow is mixed with rain here, and warm air keeps the snow level high. Whistler's best snow comes Tuesday through Wednesday, with about 11" on Wednesday alone and 32" over the window. Rain dominates from Wednesday on, so expect heavy, wet snow at the top and rain lower down.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A series of Pacific fronts brings repeated rain and mountain snow, with gusty southeast winds near the coast Monday and Tuesday. Mt. Baker and Crystal lead the snow totals, with Mt. Baker's best day on Wednesday at about 8". The Weather Prediction Center and NWS both see a wet pattern holding through the holiday weekend.

regions.title: Northern Rockies
regions.text: A passing trough brings only light snow showers to western Wyoming on Monday, then drier weather Tuesday and Wednesday. A more active pattern starts Thursday, with Jackson Hole's best day on Friday at about 6". Strong westerly winds on the Thursday-into-Friday window could gust 50 to 70 mph on eastern slopes, so check lift status.

regions.title: Kootenays
regions.text: Snow here is light and mixed with rain, with the most snow falling Thursday when it briefly turns to snow. Whitewater and Revelstoke both see their best day Thursday at about 4". Expect rain showers by Friday as the warmer air settles in.

ahead.text: The Weather Prediction Center says another round of widespread rain and breezy winds is likely Wednesday night into Thursday, with heavy rain over the Olympics. The Climate Prediction Center expects an active, progressive pattern from Saturday Nov 28 through Tuesday Dec 2.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
